title: Power and Prediction: The Disruptive Economics of Artificial Intelligence
author: Ajay Agrawal
Joshua Gans
Avi Goldfarb
target_audience: Students and scholars interested in AI and economics
General readers seeking to understand AI’s economic impact
core_themes: The economic value and limits of prediction technologies
AI’s role as a prediction tool rather than autonomous intelligence
The adjustment and disruption of business models due to AI
Organizational and institutional change required to harness AI
Barriers to AI adoption and the concept of ‘the between times’
Redefinition of power within industries due to AI integration
primary_purpose: To examine how advances in artificial intelligence, particularly in prediction, are disrupting economic structures, impacting business strategies, and shifting the balance of power among individuals, firms, and institutions.

structure_format.organization: Divided into thematic chapters that sequentially build the argument, with case studies and historical analogies
features: Diagrams illustrating economic theories and AI’s impact
Frameworks for understanding decision-making in the age of AI
Glossaries and clear definitions of key terms

key_concepts_lessons: Artificial intelligence’s core value is the dramatic improvement in prediction capabilities, but prediction is only one component of decision-making.
AI’s transformative power comes not only from technology but from reimagining organizational processes to leverage prediction tools.
The ‘between times’—a period when technology exists but institutions and processes haven’t adapted—can result in slow and uneven adoption.
AI’s disruption often creates more value by changing what firms can and should do, rather than simply automating existing processes.
Control over decision-making moves from ‘experts’ to those who control and deploy prediction technologies, shifting power within industries.
Adoption barriers are organizational and institutional, not just technical.
notable_features: Focuses on the economic and strategic implications of AI, not technical details
Uses historical analogies (e.g., the electric motor) to explain the diffusion and adoption curve of new technologies
Explores limitations and risks of relying on prediction without adequate complementary changes
cultural_historical_context: Published amid rapid expansion of AI capabilities and widespread discussion about automation, the future of work, and tech-driven inequality. Builds on the authors’ prior influential work 'Prediction Machines' and responds to concern and excitement about AI’s impact beyond the technical sphere.
reception_impact: Praised for clarifying and demystifying AI’s disruptive potential in economic and strategic terms
Adopted in business and economics curricula for its frameworks and approachable style
Influential among business strategists and policy advisors
Some critics note a heavy focus on North American markets and economic institutions
comparable_titles: Prediction Machines: The Simple Economics of Artificial Intelligence by Ajay Agrawal, Joshua Gans, and Avi Goldfarb
The Second Machine Age by Erik Brynjolfsson and Andrew McAfee
Competing in the Age of AI by Marco Iansiti and Karim R. Lakhani
